entry.title: Facility Layout and Design
entry.summary: I am taking this course in the fall of 2026, and it is teaching me to think about a factory as a whole: where every department goes, how material moves between them, and how a building has to change when a company grows or adds…
entry.content:
I am taking this course in the fall of 2026, and it is teaching me to think about a factory as a whole: where every department goes, how material moves between them, and how a building has to change when a company grows or adds a new product. Instead of designing a single workstation, I am learning to design the facility itself, starting from a clear definition of the problem and building up, step by step, the evidence needed to justify a layout.

  • The technical skills gained: 
    • Facilities Design as Engineering Design - Applying the engineering design process to facilities, and distinguishing a facility, its layout, the facility design, and the overall facilities plan.
    • Defining the Design Problem - Turning a business need into a design basis with a formal problem statement, objectives, scope and system boundary, requirements, constraints, and design criteria before proposing any layout.
    • PQRST Analysis - Gathering and interpreting the Product, Quantity, Routing, Supporting services, and Timing information a layout depends on, and translating each piece into facility requirements.
    • Material Flow Analysis - Converting production demand into physical movements and equivalent unit loads, and building from-to charts to measure the direction and intensity of flow between activities.
    • Activity Relationship Analysis - Assigning closeness ratings (A, E, I, O, U, X) backed by evidence and reason codes, converting flow intensity into closeness letters, and building Activity Relationship Charts and Diagrams with Muther's notation.
    • Computer-Aided Layout Design - Modeling facilities and workstations in 3D with SketchUp, drafting floor plans to scale in AutoCAD from real measurements, and drawing relationship diagrams in yEd.

Course Case Study: Caribe Surgical Access

 Team semester project — ININ 4040: Facilities Layout and Design (in progress)

The problem: Caribe Surgical Access (CSA) is a medical-device manufacturer in Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, that makes two single-use surgical trocars, T5 and T10, devices used to create and maintain a small opening through the abdominal wall during minimally invasive surgery. The plant molds its own plastic components, machines stainless-steel shafts, and assembles, tests, and packages each device in a 26,400 ft² building. CSA now needs to introduce a third product, T12, and grow from 192,000 to 266,400 good devices per year in Year 1 (about 39% more), reaching 325,000 by Year 5. All of this has to happen on a single shift, inside the existing building, and without moving its walls, columns, docks, or emergency exits. Our team was hired to determine what must change in the facility to handle this growth and the new product.

Our approach: Before proposing any layout, we built the design basis. We defined the problem formally, including the system boundary (from the receiving docks on the west to the shipping docks on the east), the stakeholders, the requirements, and the fixed constraints, and calculated the required pace: a takt time of 23.6 seconds per unit in Year 1 and 19.4 seconds by Year 5. We then documented the full PQRST information: the 18 part numbers and which ones are made in-house or bought, the routes of the five material streams through the plant, demand and product mix by year, and the supporting services. From there, we identified 28 facility activities and rated how close each pair should be using Muther's closeness codes. Every data point and assumption was logged in an evidence register of 45 entries, each marked as current, assumed, or still to be verified.

What we found so far:

  • Capacity is the biggest risk. A rough load check puts cannula subassembly at about 97% in Year 1 and 120% in Year 5, and the Swiss CNC lathes at about 95% and 119%, leaving little or no margin.
  • The product mix makes it harder. Demand shifts toward T12, which has the longest process times and the lowest first-pass test conformance (94.5%), so the workload grows faster than the number of units.
  • Material flow is inefficient. Each device crosses the main aisle twice and backtracks between assembly, testing, and packaging, and that 10 ft aisle carries all five material streams, mixing forklifts, pallet jacks, and carts right next to the controlled assembly room.
  • There is an opportunity. The three products share most of their architecture, T12 only adds three unique parts, and there is underused space in the building plus an 8,800 ft² expansion reserve on the north side.

Next steps: The next stage of the project is a detailed capacity calculation for each resource that includes changeovers and allowances, a from-to chart of flow intensity between activities, an activity relationship diagram, and space requirements for Years 1 and 5, which together will lead to our proposed layout.

Skills applied: Facility design problem definition, PQRST analysis, takt time, routing and material flow analysis, activity modeling, Muther's closeness ratings, capacity load analysis, evidence and assumptions register, teamwork and technical writing

entry.title: Automation and Process Control
entry.summary: I am taking this course in the fall of 2026, and it is where I get my hands on the hardware behind modern manufacturing. Instead of only analyzing systems on paper, I am learning how automated processes actually sense, decide, and act: wiring circuits, connecting…
entry.content:
I am taking this course in the fall of 2026, and it is where I get my hands on the hardware behind modern manufacturing. Instead of only analyzing systems on paper, I am learning how automated processes actually sense, decide, and act: wiring circuits, connecting sensors and actuators, and programming the controllers that run them. Most of the learning happens in the lab, where every concept from class has to work on a real breadboard, a real PLC, or a real pneumatic cylinder.

  • The technical skills gained: 
    • Automation Fundamentals - Understanding the types of automation (fixed, programmable, and flexible) and how every automated process is built from sensors, actuators, and a controller.
    • Electrical Circuits - Building series and parallel circuits on a breadboard and measuring voltage and current with a multimeter, following lab safety practices.
    • Number Systems - Working with binary, octal, and hexadecimal, the number systems used by computers and digital controllers.
    • Sensors - Connecting and testing contact sensors, photoelectric sensors, proximity sensors (reed switch, inductive, and capacitive), and fiber optics, and determining their operating distances.
    • Actuators, Relays, and Pneumatics - Wiring motors, lights, and electromagnets, using relays to control circuits, and building pneumatic systems with valves and cylinders.
    • PLC Programming - Writing ladder logic with normally open and normally closed contacts, coils, seal-in circuits, SET/RST instructions, timers, and counters, and testing programs in the Productivity Suite software and simulator.
    • Design for Automation - Applying design thinking and design for manufacture and assembly principles, including a hands-on design challenge prototyping solutions with fischertechnik components.

entry.title: Queueing Systems and Simulation
entry.summary: I am taking this course in the fall of 2026, and it is teaching me how to study systems where randomness is part of the story: customers arriving at unpredictable times, machines that break down, and processes that never take exactly the same amount of…
entry.content:
I am taking this course in the fall of 2026, and it is teaching me how to study systems where randomness is part of the story: customers arriving at unpredictable times, machines that break down, and processes that never take exactly the same amount of time twice. Instead of experimenting on a real factory or service line, I am learning to build computer simulation models of these systems, test changes safely, and use statistics to decide which design truly performs best.

  • The technical skills gained: 
    • Simulation Fundamentals - Understanding when and why to simulate, the steps of a simulation study, and how discrete-event simulation models a system as a sequence of events over time.
    • Input Modeling - Selecting and fitting probability distributions to real data so that arrivals, processing times, and failures in the model behave like the real system.
    • Random Numbers and Random Variates - Generating and testing random numbers, transforming them into values from specific distributions, and building Monte Carlo and spreadsheet simulations.
    • Discrete-Event Modeling in Simio - Building and animating models with resources, workers, vehicles, machine reliability, data tables, relational tables, entity routing, and custom processes.
    • Model Verification and Validation - Checking that a model is built correctly and that it accurately represents the real system before trusting its results.
    • Output Analysis - Analyzing terminating and steady-state simulations, building confidence intervals for performance measures, and comparing alternative system configurations to select the best one.
    • Variance Reduction Techniques - Using common random numbers and antithetic variates to get more precise comparisons from fewer simulation runs.

The Tools

Simio: Simio is the simulation software at the center of this course. It lets you build a model of a real system by placing objects such as sources, servers, conveyors, and sinks on a 3D facility view, connecting them with paths, and then watching the system run in real time. Through a series of hands-on labs, I learned to go beyond the drag-and-drop basics: storing product data in tables, routing parts by type, modeling workers, vehicles, and machine failures, and writing custom process logic for behavior the standard objects can't handle on their own. Simio also runs multiple replications of a model and reports performance measures with confidence intervals, which is what turns an animation into evidence for a decision.

Minitab: A simulation is only as good as the data that goes into it and the statistics applied to what comes out of it, and that is where Minitab comes in. I used Minitab on the input side to explore data with scatter plots, test for normality, and run goodness-of-fit tests to choose the right probability distribution for arrival and processing times. On the output side, I used it to compare system designs with statistical tests such as the two-sample t-test, the paired t-test, and ANOVA, so that a recommendation rests on real differences in performance and not on random noise.

Course Case Study: SM Electronics

 Team project — ININ 5025: Queueing Systems and Simulation (in progress)

The problem: SM Electronics, a small manufacturer of electronic parts, has three automated lines that each produce one part type (A, B, and C) and feed a fourth, shared line where the final operations are done. As the product mix shifted over time, that fourth line became a bottleneck. Parts merge onto an input conveyor that holds only 40 units, and when it fills up, incoming parts are lost, at a cost of $0.63 to $0.89 each. Inside the line, parts ride on 40 pallets through eight work cells on a loop conveyor; five cells are automated and need a setup every time the part type changes, and two are manual with variable processing times. The company is considering two costly fixes: adding pallets to the line ($17,000 plus $3,000 per pallet) or installing three new buffer conveyors that release parts in same-type batches to reduce setups ($56,000). Our team was asked to determine the weekly cost of lost production today and whether either modification, both, or neither makes economic sense.

Our approach: Because arrivals, jams, and manual processing times are all random, the interactions in this system are too complex for hand calculations alone, which makes it a good fit for simulation. We built a current-state model of the line in Simio: three part arrival streams with random jam delays, a merge onto the 40-part input conveyor that records lost parts by type, a combined load/unload station for the pallets, and seven work cells on accumulating conveyors. We stored all setup and operation times in a data table and used state variables so that each automated cell remembers the last part type it processed and only performs a setup when the type changes. Before modeling, we also ran quick hand calculations as a sanity check, which showed that with setups every automated cell takes longer per part than the time between arrivals, so a large share of parts is likely being lost today. We presented the current-state model at the project's progress presentation.

Next steps: Since the line restarts each day with unfinished parts still in place, we will treat it as a steady-state system with a warm-up period. We will then estimate the weekly cost of lost production, model both proposed modifications (including the batch release logic for the buffer conveyors), and compare all alternatives statistically to recommend the most cost-effective configuration.

Skills applied: Discrete-event simulation, Simio modeling (data tables, state variables, conveyors, combiners and separators), input modeling, steady-state output analysis, comparison of alternatives, cost analysis, teamwork and technical presentation

entry.title: Methods & Work Measurement
entry.summary: I took this course in the spring of 2026, and it is where Industrial Engineering started to feel tangible to me: instead of looking at a system from a distance, I learned to watch a person do a job, break it down motion by motion,…
entry.content:
I took this course in the spring of 2026, and it is where Industrial Engineering started to feel tangible to me: instead of looking at a system from a distance, I learned to watch a person do a job, break it down motion by motion, and figure out how long it should take and how to make it better. The course combined work systems design with work measurement, giving me the tools to evaluate, standardize, and improve the productivity and efficiency of manual operations.

  • The technical skills gained: 
    • Methods Analysis - Mapping operations with flow process charts, assembly charts, and left-hand/right-hand (operator) charts built from the 17 Therbligs, to find and eliminate wasted motions.
    • Direct Time Studies - Timing work elements with a stopwatch (snapback and continuous methods), determining the required number of cycles, and checking results with confidence intervals.
    • Performance Rating - Leveling observed times to a "normal" pace using speed rating, the Westinghouse system, and the synthetic method, and evaluating how consistent an analyst's ratings are.
    • Allowances and Standard Time - Adding personal, fatigue, and delay (PFD) allowances, including heat-stress allowances, to build labor time standards for both manual and machine-paced work.
    • Work Sampling - Estimating how workers and machines spend their time through random observations instead of continuous timing.
    • Line Balancing - Assigning work elements to stations using precedence diagrams to meet a target cycle time while minimizing idle time.
    • Predetermined Time Systems - Building time standards from motion data with MOST (general move, controlled move, and tool use sequences), without needing a stopwatch.

entry.title: Cost Management
entry.summary: Welcome to this section of my portfolio! In my journey studying Industrial Engineering at the University of Puerto Rico, Mayagüez Campus, one of the most pivotal courses I have completed is ININ 4087: Cost Management. While engineering often focuses on the physical optimization of systems,…
entry.content:
Welcome to this section of my portfolio! In my journey studying Industrial Engineering at the University of Puerto Rico, Mayagüez Campus, one of the most pivotal courses I have completed is ININ 4087: Cost Management.

While engineering often focuses on the physical optimization of systems, this class reinforced that true process optimization requires a deep understanding of financial strategy. Whether evaluating the efficiency of a vehicle assembly line, managing project budgets for a collaborative team, or analyzing a supply chain, grasping how costs behave is an essential skill for any engineer.

Here is a look at the core competencies and strategic insights I developed through this course and its culminating final project.

The Core of Cost Management: The foundation of the curriculum centered on the mechanics of financial tracking and control. We learned to identify, calculate, and analyze various types of costs, including indirect, direct, variable, and fixed.


Beyond basic accounting, the course emphasized modern cost analysis techniques crucial for continuous improvement, such as:

  • Activity-Based Costing (ABC) & Life-Cycle Costing: Methods to accurately assign costs to specific processes and evaluate the financial impact of a product from conception to disposal.
  • Target Costing & Value Engineering: Proactive approaches to designing products that meet customer expectations while remaining strictly within profitable cost boundaries.
  • Root Cause Evaluation: The analytical framework needed to investigate the causes of high costs or reduced profits in manufacturing and service environments, allowing us to design better cost management systems.

Navigating Market Structures: An eye-opening aspect of the course was exploring how external market structures dictate internal financial strategies. We analyzed theoretical models like perfect competition, where a massive amount of participants means no single entity influences the market. In this utopian scenario, companies must maximize profits strictly through internal cost reduction.


Conversely, we examined imperfect structures like monopolies and oligopolies, where a smaller number of players control pricing, availability, and competitive access. Recognizing these market dynamics is critical when forecasting the financial viability of any new engineering project.

Strategic Pricing Policies: For our final project, my team and I synthesized these concepts to analyze different pricing policies and their alignment with industry needs. The policy a company chooses must perfectly align with its product nature, cost structure, and competitive sector. We explored four primary strategies:


  • Cost-Based Pricing: This strategy calculates a baseline price to cover production and ensure a consistent margin, utilizing the break-even formula (Fixed Costs / Unit Contribution Margin). It is highly effective for traditional manufacturing and regulated industries where stable, transparent costs are necessary.
  • Value-Based Pricing: Instead of focusing strictly on internal costs, this approach determines price based on the customer's perceived value. It allows for premium pricing and is ideal for highly differentiated, innovative products like luxury goods or cutting-edge technology.
  • Demand-Based Pricing: This dynamic model adjusts prices based on market segmentation and consumer price elasticity. It maximizes revenue in environments with fluctuating demand and limited capacity, heavily utilized by airlines and ride-sharing platforms (e.g., surge pricing).
  • Competition-Based Pricing: In saturated markets with highly similar products, prices are set by benchmarking direct rivals. Strategies range from aggressive penetration pricing to price matching, helping companies maintain their market share without triggering prolonged price wars.

 

Ultimately, ININ 4087 bridged the gap between tactical resource usage and high-level profitability analysis. Presenting these strategic pricing recommendations in our final executive report underscored the importance of clearly communicating complex financial data to decision-makers. As I continue to grow as an industrial engineer, the ability to seamlessly align production costs with market realities will remain a cornerstone of my approach to system optimization.

entry.title: Applied Industrial Statistics
entry.summary: I took this course in the fall of 2025, and it taught me the main statistical concepts of Industrial Engineering, the ones that made me fall in love with what IE is. During this course, I learned the theoretical and applied background needed to develop…
entry.content:
I took this course in the fall of 2025, and it taught me the main statistical concepts of Industrial Engineering, the ones that made me fall in love with what IE is. During this course, I learned the theoretical and applied background needed to develop and effectively use statistical and probabilistic models for decision making in engineering.

  • The technical skills gained: 
    • Regression Analysis - Building and validating statistical models to predict outcomes, including handling multicollinearity.
    • Design of Experiments - Testing whether or not different conditions/treatments actually produce different results.
    • Goodness-of-fit testing: Assessing if real-world data matches a theoretical distribution to understand its behavior. 

Final Course Project: Regression Analysis for Utility Planning

 Team project — ININ 4020: Applied Industrial Statistics

The problem: A utility company (Lux Inc.) wanted to better understand what drives daily energy consumption across the buildings it serves, with the goal of offering personalized efficiency recommendations and improving resource allocation. My team and I were given a dataset of 80 buildings, including square footage, occupancy, appliance load, average temperature, building type, and day of the week, and tasked with building a model that could reliably predict energy usage from these characteristics.

Our approach: Rather than jumping straight to a "final" model, we built it in stages, starting simple and adding complexity only when it was justified by the data. We began with a baseline model using just the physical characteristics of each building, then progressively layered in environmental effects (temperature), behavioral patterns (weekday vs. weekend usage), and interaction effects between variables, testing at each step whether the added complexity was actually earning its keep.

We validated each model using ANOVA, t-tests for individual predictors, and residual diagnostics (normal probability plots, versus-fits plots) to check that our assumptions held up. We used variance inflation factors (VIF) to make sure our predictors weren't dangerously correlated with each other. All analysis was done in Minitab.

Results:

  • Square footage was the single strongest driver of energy use. Bigger buildings consistently use more energy, no surprise there.
  • Building type mattered a lot: industrial buildings carry a much higher baseline energy demand than commercial or residential buildings, regardless of size.
  • Each additional appliance added roughly 20 kWh to daily consumption.
  • Energy use reliably dropped on weekends, capturing real behavioral patterns in how buildings are used.
  • Temperature had a smaller, but still statistically significant, effect; colder days used more energy than warmer ones, suggesting heating costs outweigh cooling costs in this dataset.

The judgment call: Our most technically "perfect" model (Model 5) achieved a 100% R² and virtually zero prediction error; but it also included two interaction terms that didn't meaningfully improve accuracy in practice. We recommended a simpler model (Model 4) for Lux Inc.'s actual field use instead, applying Occam's Razor: if two models explain the data equally well, the simpler one is the better choice for real-world decision-making. 

Skills applied: Multiple linear regression, ANOVA, residual diagnostics, multicollinearity assessment (VIF), model selection, Minitab, data-driven business recommendations

Regression Analysis Project

entry.title: Ergonomics and Human Factors
entry.summary: Ergonomics and Human Factors taught me that whether analyzing an assembly line or designing a new control interface, my goal should be to adapt the work to the worker. Here is a look at the methodologies and principles I used to make that happen. The…
entry.content:
Ergonomics and Human Factors taught me that whether analyzing an assembly line or designing a new control interface, my goal should be to adapt the work to the worker. Here is a look at the methodologies and principles I used to make that happen.

The Physiology and Biomechanics of Work: Before designing a task, we must understand the physical limits of the human body. By measuring maximum oxygen consumption ($VO_2\text{Max}$) and analyzing heart rate reserves (utilizing the formula $HR_{\text{Max}} = 220 - \text{Edad}$), we can determine a worker's physical capacity to perform sustained tasks without risking overexertion. Understanding spinal biomechanics allows us to classify physical workloads and design tasks that prevent the chronic lower back pain that plagues so many industrial workers.


Quantifying Ergonomic Risk: Guesswork is not an option when worker safety is on the line. I learned to apply rigorous quantitative tools to evaluate manual material handling:


  • The NIOSH Lifting Equation: By calculating the Recommended Weight Limit ($RWL$) for two-handed manual lifting tasks, we establish the maximum safe weight for a specific environment. Calculating the Lifting Index ($LI$) allows us to immediately flag high-risk tasks that require structural redesigns.
  • Snook-Ciriello Tables: For tasks involving pushing, pulling, or carrying, we utilize these psychophysical tables (developed by Liberty Mutual) to ensure that the required forces remain acceptable for the vast majority of the workforce.

Bridging Mind and Machine (Human Factors): Physical safety is only half the equation. Human error accounts for 70% to 90% of industrial accidents, and these errors are often the direct result of poor design. Through Cognitive Engineering, I learned to design control panels and interfaces that align with natural human expectations—also known as population stereotypes.


By applying concepts like Warrick's Principle and ensuring strong stimulus-response compatibility, we can build systems where the right action feels intuitive. Furthermore, designing the physical resistance of controls (such as elastic, static sliding, or viscous resistance) provides tactile feedback that reduces cognitive load and prevents costly mistakes.

Controlling the Environment and Hazards:

A safe workstation extends to the surrounding environment. I gained the skills to design comprehensive Industrial Hygiene controls, including:

  • Acoustic Management: Evaluating noise exposure against OSHA's 90 dB Permissible Exposure Limit (PEL) using dosimeters and sound level meters, and implementing Hearing Conservation Programs when necessary.
  • Lighting Optimization: Balancing illuminance (measured in footcandles or lux) and minimizing direct and indirect glare to ensure workers can perform precision tasks safely and comfortably.

Implementing Real Solutions: Ultimately, these analyses culminate in the application of the Hierarchy of Controls. The goal is always to eliminate or substitute hazards first. When that isn't possible, we rely on engineering controls to isolate the worker from the risk. For example, this includes selecting hand tools that weigh under 3 pounds for continuous use, utilizing bent-handle designs to maintain neutral wrist postures, and deploying anti-vibration technology to prevent musculoskeletal disorders.

entry.title: Design and Analysis of Engineering Experiments
entry.summary: Course Foundations & Skills Mastered Rather than just learning statistical theories, this class provided a rigorous framework for identifying where variations happen and how to systematically tune a process to hit optimal targets. It taught me how to turn raw statistical concepts into actionable engineering…
entry.content:
Course Foundations & Skills Mastered

Rather than just learning statistical theories, this class provided a rigorous framework for identifying where variations happen and how to systematically tune a process to hit optimal targets. It taught me how to turn raw statistical concepts into actionable engineering decisions. Here is a breakdown of my core takeaways:

Skill Area Practical Application
Statistical Analysis
Running hypothesis tests and calculating confidence intervals to accurately evaluate sampling errors in a given process.
Experimental Design
Setting up randomized blocks, Latin squares, and split plots to control nuisance factors and manage everyday variability.
Factorial Models
Building out two-level fractional and full factorial designs to figure out which factors actually matter and how they interact with each other.
Response Optimization
Using response surface methodology and Central Composite Designs (CCD) to measure curvature and find the mathematical "sweet spot" for a target.

Software & Analytical Tools

To bring these models to life and handle the heavy lifting of data analysis, I relied on a strong technical stack to design and validate our experiments:

  • Minitab: This was my go-to for executing ANOVA, generating Pareto charts, mapping out main effects, and running rigorous residual tests to make sure our models were actually adequate.

Real-World Application: Cart Acceleration Simulation

To put all these methodologies to the test, my team built an in-silico experiment simulating a gravity-driven cart system. The goal was to figure out the safest, most efficient way to transfer manufacturing materials between stations. We specifically looked at how the ramp angle, friction coefficient, and cart mass influenced the cart's acceleration.

  • We built a full factorial design (with center points) and completely randomized our run order to make sure the simulator's timing quirks wouldn't introduce measurement errors.
  • We calculated our response variables using the Successive Difference Method, governed by the equation a = [(x4 + x5 + x6) - (x1 + x2 + x3)] / 9t2.
  • The data proved that a steeper ramp naturally spiked acceleration, while friction pushed back hard as a direct opposing force—essentially letting us map out Newton's Second Law statistically.
  • After spotting some significant curvature in our initial data, we scaled up to a 40-run Central Composite Design. We ultimately found a lack of fit at the extreme limits, which was a great lesson in recognizing when a physical system is just too complex to be boxed into a standard quadratic model and requires non-linear regression instead.

Industrial Value & Process Optimization

Being able to statistically validate a system instead of relying on trial-and-error is everything in modern manufacturing. These Design of Experiments (DOE) methodologies directly translate to the hands-on challenges I tackle on the floor—whether that means using data to drive cycle time reductions, evaluating work content, or pushing for continuous improvement and process optimization on a vehicle assembly line.

Design of Engineering Experiments Final Project

entry.title: Production Systems and Inventory Management
entry.summary: I took this course in the spring of 2026, and it showed me how a company decides what to make, how much, and when. Starting from a forecast and working all the way down to the materials and machine hours needed on the shop floor,…
entry.content:
I took this course in the spring of 2026, and it showed me how a company decides what to make, how much, and when. Starting from a forecast and working all the way down to the materials and machine hours needed on the shop floor, I learned the analytical tools used to design and improve production and inventory systems, and how every planning decision trades off cost, capacity, and customer service.

  • The technical skills gained: 
    • Production Systems Fundamentals - Distinguishing manufacturing environments (make-to-stock, assemble-to-order, make-to-order), push versus pull systems, and the role of bottlenecks, WIP, takt time, and Lean principles.
    • Forecasting - Building and evaluating demand forecasts with moving averages, exponential smoothing, trend models, and Winters' method for seasonal data, and measuring their accuracy with MAD, MSE, and MAPE.
    • Inventory Control - Determining how much to order and when using the EOQ and EPQ models for known demand, the newsvendor model for one-time decisions, and reorder point systems with Type 1 and Type 2 service levels for uncertain demand.
    • Aggregate Planning - Developing production and workforce plans (chase, level, and mixed strategies) and optimizing them with linear programming in Excel Solver.
    • Master Production Scheduling - Translating the aggregate plan into a schedule for specific products and calculating available-to-promise (ATP) quantities for customer orders.
    • Material Requirements Planning (MRP) - Exploding bills of materials to plan component orders, comparing lot-sizing rules, and choosing the option with the lowest total cost.
    • Capacity Planning - Checking whether a production plan is feasible with the available machines and labor, using overall factors (CPOF), resource profiles, and capacity requirements planning (CRP).

entry.title: Deterministic Models in Operations Research
entry.summary: I took this course in the spring of 2026, and it taught me how to turn a messy real-world decision into a mathematical model and find the best possible answer. I learned to recognize, formulate, and solve linear optimization problems, from deciding how much of…
entry.content:
I took this course in the spring of 2026, and it taught me how to turn a messy real-world decision into a mathematical model and find the best possible answer. I learned to recognize, formulate, and solve linear optimization problems, from deciding how much of each product to make to routing shipments through a network, and, just as importantly, how to interpret the results and turn them into practical recommendations.

  • The technical skills gained: 
    • Linear Programming Formulation - Translating real-world problems such as production, blending, diet, staff scheduling, and capital budgeting into decision variables, an objective function, and constraints.
    • Graphical and Simplex Methods - Solving LP problems graphically and with the simplex algorithm (including the Big-M method), and identifying special cases such as infeasible, unbounded, and alternative optimal solutions.
    • Duality and Sensitivity Analysis - Using the dual problem and sensitivity reports to understand how much each resource is worth and how far costs or capacities can change before the optimal solution changes.
    • Computer-Based Optimization - Building and solving LP models in Excel Solver and interpreting its output.
    • Transportation, Assignment, and Transshipment Problems - Finding the lowest-cost way to ship goods from supply points to demand points, and assigning workers to tasks optimally with the Hungarian method.
    • Network Optimization - Solving shortest path problems with Dijkstra's algorithm, as well as maximum flow and minimum spanning tree problems.
    • Project Management - Scheduling projects and identifying their critical activities with the Critical Path Method (CPM) and PERT.
